svg.text: Diabetic emergencies: fast and sweaty, or slow and dry
HYPOGLYCAEMIA — below 4 mmol/L
Onset in MINUTES
Sweating, trembling, hunger
Pallor, palpitations, anxiety
Confusion, slurred speech, aggression
Then seizures and coma
CONSCIOUS: 15 to 20 g fast sugar,
recheck in 15 min, then a long-acting snack
UNCONSCIOUS: nothing by mouth — IV glucose
DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS
Onset over HOURS to DAYS
Thirst, polyuria, weight loss
Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
Deep sighing breathing (Kussmaul)
Acetone smell on the breath
DRY skin and tongue, sunken eyes
Treatment order: FLUID first, then insulin,
then potassium, and hunt for the trigger
The discriminator when you are unsure
SWEATY and RAPID onset means low sugar. DRY and SLOW onset means high sugar with ketones.
If you genuinely cannot tell and cannot measure, treat as HYPOGLYCAEMIA.
Sugar given to a hyperglycaemic patient does little harm in minutes. Sugar withheld from a hypo causes brain injury.
Potassium in DKA — the killer nobody sees
The starting potassium often looks NORMAL or HIGH, because acidosis has pushed it out of the cells.
Total body potassium is actually very LOW. Insulin then drives it back into the cells, and the level crashes.
So potassium is replaced early and monitored closely, even when the first result looks reassuring.
Watch the ECG and the urine output. Insulin is not started if potassium is below 3.5 until replacement is running.
